title: How To Handle The Uncertainty Of Next School Year
author: Michael Linsin
summary: Writing amid unresolved plans for reopening schools, Linsin lists the many unanswered practical questions worrying teachers — double lesson-planning, quarantine protocols, mask enforcement, restroom sanitation — and validates the frustration behind them while arguing against dwelling on the unknown. His central point is that a strong classroom management plan gives teachers a stable foundation regardless of whatever specific protocols eventually land, since the fundamentals of defining and defending boundaries around behavior have held constant through decades of policy churn. Drawing on thirty years of teaching, he argues no new procedure has ever shaken solid classroom management or disrupted a teacher's ability to build relationships with students, and closes by advising teachers to spend the remaining summer resting rather than pre-worrying about details that are still likely to change.
points: It's normal to feel high stress from a long list of unresolved reopening questions, but most are still out of a teacher's control.
One key to avoiding stress is not concerning yourself with matters entirely outside your control.
A strong classroom management plan provides stability regardless of whatever specific Covid protocols eventually emerge.
In thirty years of teaching, no new policy or protocol has ever managed to shake the foundations of solid classroom management.
Spend remaining summer time resting and recharging rather than pre-worrying about details still likely to change.
quotes: It’s understandable. There is so much we don’t know, so many hows, whys, and what ifs.
It does you no good to worry about things that may never come to pass. Furthermore, unless you’re in a position of leadership, it’s out of your hands.
One of the keys to avoiding stress is to not concern yourself with anything out of your control.
You see, with a strong classroom management plan, and the confidence in knowing that you can bring peace to your classroom no matter what comes your way, there is really nothing to worry about.
In 30 years of teaching, I’ve seen a zillion new procedures, policies, and protocols come down the pike and not one of them has managed to shake the foundations of good solid classroom management.
Enjoy your time off. Sleep in. Spend more time with family and good books (and bad TV). Have an adult beverage.
